title: First Epilogue (1813 - 20) — Chapter 4
paragraphs: The flood of nations begins to subside into its ordinary channels. The waves of the great movement die down, and on the now-calm surface eddies form, and in them float the diplomats, who imagine that it is they who have made the flood subside.

But the smooth sea suddenly grows troubled again. The diplomats think their own disagreements are the cause of this fresh pressure of natural forces; they expect war between their sovereigns; the situation looks to them insoluble. But the wave they feel rising does not come from the direction they expect. It rises again from the same point as before—Paris. This is the last backwash of the movement from the west, a backwash that settles the diplomatic difficulties that had seemed insoluble and brings to an end the military movement of that period of history.

The man who laid France waste returns to France alone, with no conspiracy behind him and no soldiers. Any guard could arrest him, but by strange chance no one does, and everyone rapturously greets the man they had cursed the day before and will curse again a month later.
This man is still needed, to give the final collective act its justification.
That act is performed.
The last role is played out. The actor is told to take off his costume and wash off his powder and paint: he will not be needed again.

And some years pass in which, alone on his island, he plays out a pitiful comedy to himself, justifying his own actions with intrigues and lies now that no justification is needed any longer, and showing the whole world exactly what it was that people had mistaken for strength, all the while an unseen hand was directing his actions.
The stage manager, having brought the drama to a close and stripped the actor bare, shows him to us.
"See what you believed in! Here he is! Do you understand now that it was not he but I who moved you?"
But people were dazed by the force of the movement, and it was long before they understood this.
A still greater coherence, a still greater inevitability, is to be seen in the life of Alexander I, the man who stood at the head of the countermovement from east to west.
What was needed in the man who, towering above the rest, was to stand at the head of that movement from east to west?

What was needed was a sense of justice, and a sympathy with the affairs of Europe—but a distant sympathy, not blunted by petty interests; a moral superiority over the sovereigns of the day who worked alongside him; a mild and attractive personal character; and a personal grievance against Napoleon. And all of this was found in Alexander I; all of it had been prepared by countless so-called chances of his life: his upbringing, his early liberalism, the advisers who surrounded him, and Austerlitz, and Tilsit, and Erfurt.

During the national war he took no active part, because he was not needed then. But the moment the need arose for a general European war, he appeared in his place at precisely the right moment, and, uniting the nations of Europe, led them to the goal.
The goal is reached. After the final war of 1815, Alexander holds all the power there is to hold. How does he use it?

Alexander I—the pacifier of Europe, the man who from his earliest years had striven for nothing but his people's welfare, the originator of the liberal reforms in his own country—now, when he seemed to possess the utmost power and therefore the means to bring about the welfare of his peoples, at the very time when Napoleon in exile was drawing up childish and dishonest plans for how he would have made mankind happy had he kept his power—Alexander I, having fulfilled his mission and feeling the hand of God upon him, suddenly recognizes the insignificance of that supposed power, turns away from it, and hands it over to men he despises as contemptible, saying only:
"Not unto us, not unto us, but unto Thy name!... I too am a man like the rest of you. Let me live like a man, and think of my own soul and of God."

As the sun and every atom of ether is a sphere complete in itself, and yet at the same time only a part of a whole too immense for man to grasp, so every individual carries within himself his own aims, and yet carries them in order to serve a general purpose that is beyond man's comprehension.

A bee lands on a flower and stings a child. The child is now afraid of bees, and declares that bees exist in order to sting people. A poet admires the bee drawing from the cup of a flower, and says it exists to drink in the fragrance of flowers. A beekeeper, watching the bee gather pollen from flowers and carry it to the hive, says it exists to gather honey. Another beekeeper, who has studied the life of the hive more closely, says the bee gathers pollen to feed the young bees and rear a queen, and that it exists to perpetuate its kind. A botanist notices that the bee, carrying the pollen of a male flower to a pistil, fertilizes it, and in this he sees the purpose of the bee's existence. Another botanist, watching how plants migrate, notices that the bee helps in that process, and may say that this is where the bee's purpose lies. But the ultimate purpose of the bee is not exhausted by the first of these explanations, or the second, or any of the processes the human mind is able to make out. The higher human understanding rises in uncovering these purposes, the more plainly it becomes clear that the ultimate purpose is beyond our grasp.
All that is accessible to man is the relation of the bee's life to other manifestations of life. And it is the same with the purpose behind historical figures and nations.

title: First Epilogue (1813 - 20) — Chapter 5
paragraphs: Natasha's wedding to Bezukhov, which took place in 1813, was the last happy event in the old Rostov family. Count Ilya Rostov died that same year, and, as always happens, once the father died the family broke apart.

The events of the previous year—the burning of Moscow, the flight from it, the death of Prince Andrew, Natasha's despair, Petya's death, and the old countess's grief—had fallen blow after blow on the old count's head. He seemed unable to grasp the meaning of it all, and bowed his old head, in a spiritual sense, as though expecting and even inviting further blows that would finish him off. At times he seemed frightened and distracted, and at other times unnaturally animated and full of plans.

Arranging Natasha's marriage occupied him for a while. He ordered dinners and suppers, and plainly tried to appear cheerful, but his cheerfulness was no longer infectious as it used to be: on the contrary, it stirred pity in those who knew and loved him.

When Pierre and his wife had left, he grew very quiet and began complaining of low spirits. A few days later he fell ill and took to his bed. From the start he understood he would never rise from it again, whatever encouragement the doctor gave him. The countess spent a fortnight in an armchair by his pillow without once undressing. Every time she gave him his medicine, he sobbed and silently kissed her hand. On his last day, sobbing, he asked her and his absent son to forgive him for having squandered their property—that being the one fault he was conscious of above all others. After receiving communion and unction he quietly died, and the next day a crowd of acquaintances came to pay their last respects to the deceased and filled the house the Rostovs were renting. All these acquaintances, who had so often dined and danced at his table and so often laughed at him, now said, with a shared feeling of self-reproach and emotion, as though excusing themselves: "Well, whatever he may have been, he was a most worthy man. You don't meet men like that nowadays.... And which of us hasn't weaknesses of our own?"
It was just when the count's affairs had become so tangled that no one could say what would happen if he lived another year that he unexpectedly died.

Nicholas was with the Russian army in Paris when the news of his father's death reached him. He resigned his commission at once, and without waiting for it to be accepted, took leave and went to Moscow. The state of the count's affairs became fully clear a month after his death, and it surprised everyone: the total of small debts, none of which anyone had suspected, was enormous. The debts came to double the value of the property.

Friends and relatives advised Nicholas to decline the inheritance. But he regarded such a refusal as a slur on his father's memory, which he held sacred, and so he would not even consider refusing, and accepted the inheritance along with the obligation to pay the debts.

The creditors, who had held their peace for so long, restrained while the count lived by a vague but powerful influence his careless good nature had over them, now all moved to enforce their claims at once. As always happens in such cases, a race sprang up over who should get paid first, and those who, like Mitenka, held promissory notes that had been given them as gifts now became the most demanding creditors of all. Nicholas was allowed no respite and no peace, and the very people who had seemed to pity the old man—the cause of their losses, if losses they were—now pursued the young heir without mercy, though he had taken on the debts of his own free will and plainly bore no guilt for having contracted them.

Not one of the plans Nicholas tried succeeded; the estate was sold at auction for half its value, and half the debts still remained unpaid. Nicholas accepted thirty thousand rubles that his brother-in-law Bezukhov offered him, to pay off the debts he regarded as genuinely owed for value received. And to avoid being imprisoned for the rest, as the creditors were threatening, he went back into government service.

He could not rejoin the army, where he would have been made colonel at the next vacancy, because his mother now clung to him as her one hold on life; and so, despite his reluctance to remain in Moscow among people who had known him before, and despite his loathing of the civil service, he took a post in that service in Moscow, put off the uniform he had loved so much, and moved with his mother and Sonya into a small house on Sivtsev Vrazhok.

Natasha and Pierre were living in Petersburg at the time and had no clear idea of Nicholas's circumstances. Having borrowed money from his brother-in-law, Nicholas tried to hide his wretched situation from him. His position was made all the harder because on a salary of twelve hundred rubles he had to keep not only himself but his mother and Sonya as well, while also shielding his mother from any knowledge of their poverty. The countess could not conceive of life without the luxury she had known since childhood, and, unable to grasp how hard things were for her son, kept demanding now a carriage—which they no longer kept—to send for a friend, now some expensive delicacy for herself, or wine for her son, or money to buy a surprise present for Natasha or Sonya, or for Nicholas himself.

Sonya kept the house, waited on her aunt, read to her, put up with her whims and her secret ill will, and helped Nicholas conceal their poverty from the old countess. Nicholas felt himself hopelessly in Sonya's debt for all she did for his mother, and he greatly admired her patience and devotion, but he tried to keep his distance from her.

In his heart he seemed to reproach her for being too perfect—for there being nothing in her to find fault with. She had everything people are valued for, but little that could make him love her. He felt that the more he valued her, the less he loved her. He had taken her at her word when she wrote releasing him from their engagement, and now he behaved as if everything that had once passed between them had long been forgotten and could never, under any circumstances, be revived.

Nicholas's situation went from bad to worse. The idea of setting anything aside out of his salary proved to be a dream. Not only did he save nothing, but to satisfy his mother's demands he even ran up some small debts of his own. He could see no way out of this situation. The idea of marrying some rich woman, which his female relatives kept suggesting to him, was repugnant to him. The other way out—his mother's death—never entered his mind. He wanted nothing and hoped for nothing, and deep in his heart he found a grim, stern satisfaction in enduring his situation without complaint. He tried to avoid old acquaintances with their pity and their offensive offers of help; he avoided every distraction and amusement, and even at home did nothing but play cards with his mother, pace silently up and down the room, and smoke pipe after pipe. He seemed to nurse, deliberately, the gloomy mood that alone made it possible for him to bear his situation.

title: First Epilogue (1813 - 20) — Chapter 6
paragraphs: At the start of winter, Princess Mary came to Moscow. From what was being said around town, she learned how the Rostovs were placed, and how "the son has sacrificed himself for his mother," as people put it.

"I never expected anything else of him," Princess Mary said to herself, feeling a joyful surge of her love for him. Remembering the close, friendly terms she had once had with the whole Rostov family, terms that had made her almost one of them, she felt it her duty to go and see them. But remembering her dealings with Nicholas in Voronezh, she was shy about doing it. It took a great effort, but she did go to call on them a few weeks after arriving in Moscow.

Nicholas was the first to meet her, since the countess's room could only be reached through his. But instead of the pleasure she had expected, at his very first glance at her his face took on a cold, stiff, proud expression she had never seen on it before. He asked after her health, showed her the way to his mother's room, and, after sitting there for five minutes, left.

When the princess came out of the countess's room, Nicholas met her again and, with marked formality and stiffness, escorted her to the anteroom. To her remarks about his mother's health he made no reply at all. "What business is that of yours? Leave me in peace," his look seemed to say.

"Why does she come prowling around here? What does she want? I can't stand these ladies and all their civilities!" he said aloud in Sonya's presence, evidently unable to hold back his irritation, once the princess's carriage had driven off.
"Oh, Nicholas, how can you talk like that?" cried Sonya, scarcely able to hide her delight. "She's so kind, and Mamma is so fond of her!"
Nicholas made no reply and tried to avoid speaking of the princess again. But after her visit the old countess brought her up several times a day.
She sang the princess's praises, insisted her son must call on her, said she wanted to see her often—yet always grew ill-humored the moment she began to talk about her.
Nicholas tried to stay silent whenever his mother spoke of the princess, but his silence irritated her.
"She is a very admirable, excellent young woman," she would say, "and you must go and call on her. You would at least be seeing someone, and I think it must be dull for you seeing no one but us."
"But I don't in the least want to, Mamma."
"You used to want to, and now you don't. Really, I don't understand you, my dear. One day you're bored, and the next you refuse to see anyone."
"But I never said I was bored."

"Why, you said yourself you don't even want to see her. She's a very admirable young woman, and you always liked her, but now suddenly some notion or other has gotten into your head. You hide everything from me."
"Not at all, Mamma."

"If I were asking you to do something unpleasant, that would be one thing—but I'm only asking you to return a call. One would think plain politeness required it.... Well, I've asked you, and now I won't press it any further, since you keep secrets from your own mother."
"Very well, then, I'll go, if you wish it."
"It's nothing to me. I only wish it for your sake."
Nicholas sighed, bit his mustache, and laid out the cards for a game of patience, trying to turn his mother's attention to something else.
The same conversation was repeated the next day, and the day after, and the day after that.
After her visit to the Rostovs and her unexpectedly cold reception from Nicholas, Princess Mary admitted to herself that she had been right not to want to be the first to call.

"I expected nothing else," she told herself, calling her pride to her aid. "I have nothing to do with him, and I only wanted to see the old lady, who was always kind to me and to whom I owe a great deal."

But these thoughts could not set her at ease; something like remorse troubled her whenever she thought of that visit. Though she had firmly resolved not to call on the Rostovs again and to forget the whole matter, she felt out of sorts the entire time. And when she asked herself what was distressing her, she had to admit it was her relationship with Rostov. His cold, polite manner did not reflect his real feeling for her—that much she knew—but it concealed something, and until she could discover what that something was, she felt she could not be at ease.

One day in the depths of winter, while she was sitting in the schoolroom, seeing to her nephew's lessons, she was told that Rostov had called. Firmly resolved not to give herself away or show any agitation, she sent for Mademoiselle Bourienne and went with her to the drawing room.
Her first glance at Nicholas's face told her that he had come only to satisfy the demands of politeness, and she firmly resolved to match the tone in which he addressed her.

They spoke of the countess's health, of mutual friends, of the latest news from the war, and when the ten minutes propriety required had passed, after which a visitor may rise, Nicholas got up to say goodbye.

With Mademoiselle Bourienne's help the princess had kept the conversation going quite well, but at the very last moment, just as he rose, she grew so weary of talking about things that did not interest her, and her mind was so full of the question of why she alone had been granted so little happiness in life, that in a fit of absent-mindedness she sat still, her luminous eyes fixed straight ahead of her, not noticing that he had stood up.

Nicholas glanced at her and, wanting to seem not to notice her distraction, made some remark to Mademoiselle Bourienne and then looked at the princess again. She still sat motionless, a look of suffering on her gentle face. He suddenly felt sorry for her, and had a vague sense that he might be the cause of the sadness written on her face. He wanted to help her, to say something kind, but he could think of nothing to say.
"Goodbye, Princess!" he said.
She started, flushed, and sighed deeply.
"Oh, I beg your pardon," she said, as if waking up. "Are you leaving already, Count? Well then, goodbye! Oh, but the cushion for the countess!"
"Wait a moment, I'll fetch it," said Mademoiselle Bourienne, and she left the room.
They both sat in silence, with only an occasional glance at one another.

"Yes, Princess," Nicholas said at last, with a sad smile, "it doesn't seem so long ago since we first met at Bogucharovo, but how much water has flowed under the bridge since then! What distress we all seemed to be in then, and yet I would give a great deal to bring that time back... but there's no bringing it back."

Princess Mary gazed intently into his eyes with her own luminous ones as he said this. She seemed to be trying to fathom the hidden meaning behind his words, one that would explain his feelings for her.

"Yes, yes," she said, "but you have no reason to regret the past, Count. As I understand your present life, I think you'll always look back on it with satisfaction, because the self-sacrifice that fills it now..."
"I can't accept your praise," he interrupted hurriedly. "On the contrary, I keep reproaching myself.... But this isn't at all an interesting or cheerful subject."
His face resumed its former stiff, cold expression. But the princess had caught a glimpse of the man she had known and loved, and it was to that man that she now spoke.

"I thought you would let me say this," she said. "I had come so close to you... and to all your family, that I thought you wouldn't consider my sympathy out of place, but I was mistaken," and suddenly her voice trembled. "I don't know why," she went on, collecting herself, "but you used to be different, and..."
"There are a thousand reasons why," he said, laying a particular emphasis on the word why. "Thank you, Princess," he added softly. "Sometimes it's hard."

"So that's why! That's why!" a voice whispered in Princess Mary's soul. "No, it wasn't only that cheerful, kind, open look, not only that handsome exterior, that I loved in him. I sensed his noble, resolute, self-sacrificing spirit too," she told herself. "Yes, he is poor now, and I am rich.... Yes, that's the only reason.... Yes, if it weren't for that..." And remembering his former tenderness, and looking now at his kind, sorrowful face, she suddenly understood the cause of his coldness.
"But why, Count, why?" she almost cried, unconsciously moving closer to him. "Why? Tell me. You must tell me!"
He said nothing.

"I don't understand your why, Count," she went on, "but it's hard for me... I confess it. For some reason you want to rob me of our old friendship. And that hurts me." There were tears in her eyes and in her voice. "I've had so little happiness in life that every loss is hard for me to bear.... Forgive me, goodbye!" and suddenly she began to cry and hurried from the room.
"Princess, for God's sake!" he exclaimed, trying to stop her. "Princess!"
She turned around. For a few seconds they gazed silently into each other's eyes—and what had seemed impossible and remote suddenly became possible, inevitable, and very near.

title: First Epilogue (1813 - 20) — Chapter 7
paragraphs: In the winter of 1813 Nicholas married Princess Mary and moved to Bald Hills with his wife, his mother, and Sonya.

Within four years he had paid off all his remaining debts without selling any of his wife's property, and after receiving a small inheritance on the death of a cousin, he paid off his debt to Pierre as well.

Within another three years, by 1820, he had managed his affairs so well that he was able to buy a small estate next to Bald Hills, and was now negotiating to buy back Otradnoe—the one thing he dreamed of above all else.

Having taken up farming out of necessity, he grew so devoted to it that it became his favorite, almost his only, occupation. Nicholas was a plain, practical farmer: he had no love for innovations, especially the English ones then coming into fashion. He laughed at theoretical treatises on estate management, disliked factories, disliked the raising of expensive crops or the buying of expensive seed corn, and made no particular hobby of any single branch of the work on his estate. He always kept the whole estate before his mind's eye, never any one part of it in isolation. The thing that mattered most to him was not the nitrogen in the soil, or the oxygen in the air, or manure, or a particular kind of plow, but that most important agent through which nitrogen, oxygen, manure, and plow were all made effective in the first place—the peasant laborer. When Nicholas first took up farming and began to understand its different branches, it was the serf above all who caught his attention. To him the peasant was not merely a tool, but also a judge of farming, and an end in himself. At first he watched the serfs, trying to understand what they were aiming at and what they thought good or bad, and he only pretended to be directing and ordering them, while in reality learning from them their methods, their manner of speaking, and their sense of what was good and what was bad. Only once he had understood the peasants' tastes and aspirations, had learned to speak their language, had grasped the hidden meaning behind their words, and felt himself akin to them, did he begin to manage his serfs with confidence—that is, to carry out toward them the duties expected of him. And Nicholas's management produced very brilliant results.

Guided by some gift for reading people, the moment he took over management of the estates he unerringly appointed as bailiff, village elder, and delegate, exactly the men the serfs themselves would have chosen had they had the right to choose, and these men never lost their posts. Before he analyzed the properties of manure, before he went into the debit and credit, as he ironically called it, he found out how many head of cattle the peasants had, and increased the number by every means available. He kept the peasant families together in the largest groups possible, never allowing family groups to split into separate households. He came down hard on the lazy, the corrupt, and the weak alike, and tried to have them expelled from the commune.

He was as careful over the sowing and reaping of the peasants' hay and corn as he was over his own, and few landowners had their crops sown and harvested so early and so well, or got so good a return, as Nicholas did.

He disliked having anything to do with the household serfs—the "drones," as he called them—and everyone said he spoiled them through his laxity. Whenever a decision had to be made about a household serf, especially if punishment was in question, he always felt undecided and consulted everyone in the house; but when it was possible to have a household serf conscripted in place of a field worker, he did so without a moment's hesitation. He never felt the slightest hesitation in dealing with the peasants. He knew that whatever he decided, they would approve of it almost to a man.

He never allowed himself to be hard on anyone, or to punish anyone, or to make things easier for or reward anyone, simply because he happened to feel like it. He could not have said by what standard he judged what he should or should not do, but in his own mind that standard was quite firm and definite.
Often, speaking with vexation of some failure or some piece of disorder, he would say, "What can one do with our Russian peasants?"—and would imagine that he could not stand them.

Yet he loved "our Russian peasants" and their way of life with his whole soul, and it was for that very reason that he had come to understand and make his own the one style of farming that produced good results.

Countess Mary was jealous of this passion of her husband's, and regretted that she could not share it; but she could not understand the joys and the vexations he drew from that world, so remote and so foreign to her. She could not understand why he was so unusually animated and happy when, after getting up at daybreak and spending the whole morning out in the fields or on the threshing floor, he came back from sowing or mowing or reaping to have tea with her. She did not understand why he spoke with such admiration and delight of the farming methods of the thrifty, well-to-do peasant Matthew Ermishin, who with his whole family had carted corn all night long; or of the fact that his own—Nicholas's—sheaves were already stacked before anyone else had brought their harvest in. She did not understand why he stepped out from the window onto the veranda, smiling under his mustache and winking with sheer joy, when a warm, steady rain began falling on the dry, thirsty shoots of the young oats, or why, when the wind carried a threatening storm cloud away during the hay harvest, he would come back from the barn, flushed, sunburned, and sweating, with a smell of wormwood and gentian caught in his hair, and, rubbing his hands together gleefully, say: "Well, one more day, and my grain and the peasants' will all be safely under cover."

Even less did she understand why he, kindhearted as he was and always ready to anticipate her wishes, could become almost desperate when she brought him a petition from some peasant men or women asking to be let off some piece of work; why he, that same kind Nicholas, could obstinately refuse her, angrily telling her not to interfere in what was not her business. She felt that he had a whole world apart from her, one he loved passionately, with laws of its own that she had never fathomed.

Sometimes, trying to understand him, she would talk about the good he was doing for his serfs, and he would grow vexed and reply: "Not in the least; it never even crossed my mind, and I wouldn't do it for their good! That's all poetry and old wives' tales—all this doing good to one's neighbor! What I want is for our children not to have to go begging. I have to put our affairs in order while I'm still alive, that's all. And for that, order and strictness are essential.... That's the whole of it!" he would say, clenching his powerful fist. "And fairness too, of course," he would add, "because if the peasant is naked and starving and has only one wretched horse to his name, he can't do any good either for himself or for me."

And everything Nicholas did bore fruit—probably precisely because he refused to let himself think he was doing good to others for virtue's sake. His fortune grew rapidly; serfs from neighboring estates came begging him to buy them, and long after his death the memory of his management was devoutly preserved among the serfs. "He was a real master... his peasants' affairs came first, and his own second. Of course he wasn't a man to be trifled with either—in a word, he was a real master!"

title: First Epilogue (1813 - 20) — Chapter 8
paragraphs: One matter connected with his management sometimes troubled Nicholas: his quick temper, together with his old hussar habit of making free use of his fists. At first he saw nothing wrong in it, but in the second year of his marriage his view of that kind of punishment suddenly changed.

One summer he had sent for the village elder from Bogucharovo, a man who had taken over the post after Dron died and who was accused of dishonesty and various irregularities. Nicholas went out onto the porch to question him, and almost as soon as the elder had given a few answers, the sound of shouting and blows could be heard. On returning to lunch, Nicholas went up to his wife, who sat with her head bent low over her embroidery frame, and, as usual, began telling her what he had been doing that morning. Among other things he mentioned the Bogucharovo elder. Countess Mary turned red, then pale, but went on sitting with her head bowed and her lips pressed together, and gave her husband no answer.

"Such an insolent scoundrel!" he cried, growing hot all over again at the mere memory of him. "If he'd only told me he was drunk and hadn't seen... But what's the matter with you, Mary?" he suddenly asked.
Countess Mary raised her head and tried to speak, but hastily looked down again, and her lips puckered.
"Why, whatever is the matter, my dearest?"

The plain Countess Mary's looks always improved when she was in tears. She never cried from pain or vexation, only from sorrow or pity, and when she wept her radiant eyes took on an irresistible charm.
The instant Nicholas took her hand, she could no longer hold herself back, and began to cry.
"Nicholas, I saw it... he was to blame, but why do you... Nicholas!" and she covered her face with her hands.

Nicholas said nothing. He flushed crimson, moved away from her, and paced up and down the room. He understood what she was crying about, but he could not, in his heart, at once agree with her that what he had regarded since childhood as a perfectly ordinary event was wrong. "Is this just sentimentality, old wives' talk, or is she right?" he asked himself. Before he could settle the question, he glanced at her face again, full of love and pain, and suddenly he understood that she was right, and that he had long been sinning against his own better self.
"Mary," he said softly, going up to her, "it will never happen again, I give you my word. Never," he repeated, in a trembling voice, like a boy begging forgiveness.
The tears flowed even faster from the countess's eyes. She took his hand and kissed it.
"Nicholas, when did you break your cameo?" she asked, to change the subject, looking at his finger, on which he wore a ring set with a cameo of Laocoon's head.

"Today—it happened in that same business. Oh, Mary, don't remind me of it!" and again he flushed. "I give you my word of honor it won't happen again, and let this always serve as a reminder to me," and he pointed to the broken ring.

After that, whenever the blood rushed to his face and his fists began to clench in some discussion with his village elders or stewards, Nicholas would turn the broken ring on his finger and drop his eyes before the man who was making him angry. But even so, he forgot himself once or twice within the year, and then he would go and confess to his wife, and would promise all over again that this would truly be the very last time.
"Mary, you must despise me!" he would say. "I deserve it."
"You should go away at once, if you don't feel strong enough to control yourself," she would answer sadly, trying to comfort her husband.

Among the gentry of the province, Nicholas was respected but not liked. He had no interest in the affairs of his own class, and as a result some thought him proud and others thought him stupid. The whole summer, from spring sowing to harvest, he was busy with the work on his farm. In autumn he gave himself over to hunting with the same businesslike seriousness, leaving home for a month, or even two, with his hunting party. In winter he visited his other villages or spent his time reading. The books he read were chiefly historical, and he set aside a certain sum for them every year. He was assembling, as he put it, a serious library, and he made it a point of principle to read through every book he bought. He would sit in his study with a grave expression, reading—a task he had first imposed on himself as a duty, but which had since become a habit that gave him a particular kind of pleasure and a sense of being occupied with serious matters. In winter, apart from business trips, he spent most of his time at home, making himself part of the family and involving himself in every detail of the children's relations with their mother. The harmony between him and his wife grew closer and closer, and every day he discovered fresh spiritual riches in her.

From the time of his marriage, Sonya had lived in his house. Before the wedding, Nicholas had told his wife everything that had passed between himself and Sonya, blaming himself and praising her. He had asked Princess Mary to be gentle and kind to his cousin. She fully understood the wrong he had done Sonya, felt herself at fault toward her too, and imagined that her own wealth had swayed Nicholas's choice. She could not find any real fault with Sonya, and tried to be fond of her, but she often felt an ill will toward her that she could not overcome.
Once she had a talk with her friend Natasha about Sonya, and about her own unfairness toward her.
"You know," said Natasha, "you've read the Gospels a great deal—there's a passage in them that fits Sonya exactly."
"What passage?" asked Countess Mary, surprised.

"'For unto every one that hath shall be given, and from him that hath not shall be taken away even that which he hath.' Remember it? She's one of those who has not; why, I don't know. Maybe she just lacks selfishness, I don't know, but from her everything is taken away, everything has been taken from her. Sometimes I'm dreadfully sorry for her. I used to want so badly for Nicholas to marry her, but I always had a kind of feeling that it wouldn't happen. She's a sterile flower, you know—like some strawberry blossoms. Sometimes I feel sorry for her, and sometimes I think she doesn't feel it the way you or I would."

Though Countess Mary told Natasha that those words from the Gospel had to be understood differently, still, looking at Sonya, she found herself agreeing with Natasha's reading of them. It really did seem that Sonya did not find her position hard to bear, and had grown quite reconciled to her lot as a sterile flower. She seemed fond not so much of particular people as of the family as a whole. Like a cat, she had attached herself not to the people in the house but to the house itself. She waited on the old countess, petted and spoiled the children, was always ready to render the little services she had such a gift for, and all of it was accepted from her, without complaint but also without much gratitude.
The country house at Bald Hills had been rebuilt, though not on the same scale as under the old prince.

The buildings, begun in straitened circumstances, were more than plain. The enormous house stood on the old stone foundations but was built of wood, plastered only inside. It had bare deal floors, and was furnished with very simple, hard sofas, armchairs, tables, and chairs, made by their own serf carpenters out of their own birchwood. The house was spacious, with rooms for the household serfs and apartments for guests. Whole families of Rostov and Bolkonsky relations sometimes came to Bald Hills with sixteen horses and dozens of servants and stayed for months. Besides this, four times a year, on the name days and birthdays of the hosts, as many as a hundred guests would gather there for a day or two. The rest of the year followed its unbroken routine, with its ordinary occupations and its breakfasts, lunches, dinners, and suppers, all provided from the produce of the estate.

title: First Epilogue (1813 - 20) — Chapter 9
paragraphs: It was the eve of St. Nicholas's day, the fifth of December, 1820. Natasha had been staying at her brother's, with her husband and children, since early autumn. Pierre had gone to Petersburg on business of his own, for three weeks, he had said, but had stayed nearly seven, and was expected back at any moment.
Besides the Bezukhov family, Nicholas's old friend the retired General Vasili Dmitrich Denisov was also staying with the Rostovs on this fifth of December.

On the sixth, which was his name day, when the house would be full of guests, Nicholas knew he would have to trade his Tartar tunic for a tailcoat, put on narrow, pointed-toe boots, drive to the new church he had built, and then receive the guests who would come to congratulate him, offer them refreshments, and talk about the nobility's elections; but he considered himself entitled to spend the eve of that day in his usual way. He went over the bailiff's accounts for the village in Ryazan that belonged to his wife's nephew, wrote two letters on business, and before dinner walked over to the granaries, the cattle yards, and the stables. Having taken precautions against the general drunkenness sure to break out the next day, since it was a great saint's day, he came back to dinner and, without having had time for a private word with his wife, sat down at the long table laid for twenty, at which the whole household had gathered. At that table sat his mother, his mother's old companion Belova, his wife, their three children with their governess and tutor, his wife's nephew with his tutor, Sonya, Denisov, Natasha, her three children with their governess, and old Michael Ivanovich, the late prince's architect, who still lived on at Bald Hills in retirement.

Countess Mary sat at the other end of the table. The moment her husband took his place, she could tell, from the quick way he pushed back the tumbler and wineglass standing in front of him after picking up his napkin, that he was out of sorts—as sometimes happened when he came in to dinner straight from the farm, especially before the soup. Countess Mary knew that mood of his well, and when she herself was in a good frame of mind, she would quietly wait until he had had his soup, and then start talking to him until she got him to admit there was no real cause for his ill humor. But today she quite forgot all that, and felt hurt that he should be angry with her for no reason, and she felt unhappy. She asked him where he had been. He answered. She asked again whether everything was going well on the farm. Her unnatural tone made him wince, and he answered quickly, almost curtly.

"Then I'm not mistaken," thought Countess Mary. "Why is he cross with me?" She concluded from his tone that he was annoyed with her and wanted to end the conversation. She knew her own remarks sounded unnatural, but she could not stop herself from asking a few more questions.

Thanks to Denisov, the conversation at the table soon turned general and lively, and she stopped talking to her husband. When they rose from the table and went, as always, to thank the old countess, Countess Mary held out her hand and kissed her husband, and asked him why he was angry with her.
"You're always imagining such strange things! I never even thought of being angry," he replied.
But the word always seemed to her to mean: "Yes, I am angry, but I won't tell you why."

Nicholas and his wife lived together so happily that even Sonya and the old countess, who were jealous and would have liked to see them disagree, could find nothing to reproach them with; and yet even they had their moments of friction. It happened most often, and always just after they had been at their happiest together, that they suddenly felt a wave of estrangement and hostility—this occurred most frequently during Countess Mary's pregnancies, and this was one such time.

"Well, mesdames et messieurs," said Nicholas loudly, with a show of cheerfulness—Countess Mary felt he was doing it on purpose to vex her—"I've been on my feet since six this morning. Tomorrow I'll have to pay for it, so today I'm going to go rest."
And without a word to his wife he went off to the little sitting room and lay down on the sofa.

"That's always the way," thought Countess Mary. "He talks to everyone but me. I see... I see that I disgust him, especially now, in this condition." She looked down at her swollen figure, and at her pale, sallow, wasted face in the mirror, in which her eyes now looked larger than ever.
And everything irritated her—Denisov's laughing and shouting, Natasha's chatter, and, above all, a quick glance Sonya gave her.
Sonya was always the first excuse Countess Mary found for feeling irritated.
Having sat a while with her guests without taking in a word of what they were saying, she quietly left the room and went to the nursery.

The children were playing at "going to Moscow" in a carriage made of chairs, and invited her to come along. She sat down and played with them a little, but her mind kept returning to her husband and his unaccountable ill temper. She got up and, walking on tiptoe with some difficulty, went to the small sitting room.
"Perhaps he's not asleep; I'll have it out with him," she told herself. Little Andrew, her eldest boy, imitating his mother, followed her on tiptoe. She did not notice him.
"Mary dear, I think he's asleep—he was so tired," said Sonya, meeting her in the large sitting room. It seemed to Countess Mary that Sonya crossed her path everywhere. "Andrew might wake him."

Countess Mary looked around, saw little Andrew following her, saw that Sonya was right, and for that very reason flushed and, with evident effort, kept herself from saying something sharp. She said nothing, but, to avoid obeying Sonya, motioned to Andrew to follow her quietly and went on to the door. Sonya left by another door. From the room where Nicholas was sleeping came the sound of his even breathing, every faint shade of which was familiar to his wife. As she listened to it, she pictured his smooth, handsome forehead, his mustache, his whole face, just as she had so often seen it in the stillness of the night while he slept. Nicholas suddenly stirred and cleared his throat. And at that very moment little Andrew shouted from behind the door: "Papa! Mamma's standing right here!" Countess Mary went white with fright and made frantic signs to the boy. He fell silent, and for a moment there was a stillness that felt terrible to Countess Mary. She knew how much Nicholas hated being woken. Then, through the door, she heard Nicholas clear his throat again and stir, and his voice said crossly:
"Can't a man get a moment's peace.... Mary, is that you? Why did you bring him in here?"
"I only came in to look, and didn't notice... forgive me...."

Nicholas coughed and said nothing more. Countess Mary drew away from the door and led the boy back to the nursery. Five minutes later, little black-eyed, three-year-old Natasha, her father's pet, having learned from her brother that Papa was asleep and Mamma was in the sitting room, ran off to her father without her mother noticing. The dark-eyed little girl boldly pushed open the creaking door, marched up to the sofa with the determined steps of her sturdy little legs, and, having studied the position of her father, who was asleep with his back to her, rose on tiptoe and kissed the hand lying under his head. Nicholas turned over, a tender smile spreading across his face.
"Natasha, Natasha!" came Countess Mary's frightened whisper from the doorway. "Papa wants to sleep."
"No, Mamma, he doesn't want to sleep," little Natasha declared with conviction. "He's laughing."
Nicholas lowered his legs, sat up, and took his daughter in his arms.
"Come in, Mary," he said to his wife.
She went in and sat down beside her husband.
"I didn't notice him following me," she said timidly. "I just looked in."
Holding his little girl in one arm, Nicholas glanced at his wife and, seeing her guilty expression, put his other arm around her and kissed her hair.
"May I kiss Mamma?" he asked Natasha.
Natasha smiled bashfully.
"Again!" she commanded, pointing with a peremptory gesture at the spot where Nicholas had planted the kiss.
"I don't know why you think I'm cross," said Nicholas, answering the question he knew was on his wife's mind.
"You have no idea how unhappy, how alone, I feel when you're like that. It always seems to me..."
"Mary, don't talk nonsense. You ought to be ashamed of yourself!" he said cheerfully.
"It seems to me that you can't love me, that I'm so plain... always... and now... in this condi..."

"Oh, how silly you are! It isn't beauty that wins love, it's love that makes us see beauty. It's only Malvinas and women like that who are loved for their beauty. But do I love my wife? I don't love her, but... I don't know how to put it. Without you, or when something comes between us like this, I feel lost and can't do anything. Now, do I love my finger? I don't love it, but just try cutting it off!"
"I'm not like that myself, but I understand. So you're not angry with me?"
"Furiously angry!" he said, smiling as he got up. And smoothing his hair, he began pacing the room.
"Do you know, Mary, what I've been thinking?" he began, immediately thinking aloud in front of his wife now that they had made up.

He did not ask whether she was ready to listen to him. It made no difference to him. A thought had occurred to him, and so it belonged to her too. And he told her of his plan to persuade Pierre to stay with them until spring.
Countess Mary listened until he had finished, made some remark, and then began thinking aloud herself. Her thoughts were about the children.

"You can already see the woman in her," she said in French, pointing to little Natasha. "You men reproach us women for being illogical. Here's our logic. I say, 'Papa wants to sleep!' and she says, 'No, he's laughing.' And she was right," said Countess Mary with a happy smile.

"Yes, yes." And Nicholas, taking his little daughter in his strong hand, lifted her high, set her on his shoulder, held her by the legs, and paced the room with her. Father and daughter both wore an expression of carefree happiness.
"But you know you might be unfair. You're too fond of this one," his wife whispered in French.
"Yes, but what am I to do?... I try not to show it..."
At that moment they heard the sound of the door pulley and footsteps in the hall and anteroom, as if someone had arrived.
"Someone has come."
"I'm sure it's Pierre. I'll go and see," said Countess Mary, and left the room.

In her absence Nicholas allowed himself to give his little daughter a gallop around the room. Out of breath, he lifted the laughing child quickly off his shoulder and pressed her to his heart. His capering reminded him of dancing, and, looking at the child's round, happy little face, he thought of what she would be like when he was an old man, taking her into society and dancing the mazurka with her, just as his own father had once danced Daniel Cooper with his daughter.

"It's him, it's him, Nicholas!" said Countess Mary, coming back into the room a few minutes later. "Now our Natasha's come to life. You should have seen how thrilled she was, and how he caught it for staying away so long. Well, come along now, quick, quick! It's time you two were separated," she added, smiling at the little girl clinging to her father.
Nicholas went out, holding the child by the hand.
Countess Mary stayed behind in the sitting room.

"I would never, never have believed one could be so happy," she whispered to herself. A smile lit up her face, but at the same time she sighed, and her deep eyes held a quiet sadness, as though, even in the midst of her happiness, she felt that there is another kind of happiness unattainable in this life, one she found herself thinking of involuntarily in that very moment.

title: First Epilogue (1813 - 20) — Chapter 10
paragraphs: Natasha had married in the early spring of 1813, and by 1820 already had three daughters, along with a son she had long wished for and was now nursing. She had grown stouter and broader, so that it was hard to recognize, in this robust, motherly woman, the slim, lively Natasha of earlier days. Her features were more defined now, and wore a calm, soft, serene expression. Gone from her face was the ever-glowing animation that used to burn there and had once made up its charm. Now, her face and body were often all that could be seen of her; her soul was not visible at all. All that struck the eye was a strong, handsome, fertile woman. The old fire kindled in her face only very rarely now. It happened only when, as on this particular day, her husband came home, or a sick child was on the mend, or when she and Countess Mary spoke of Prince Andrew—she never mentioned him to her own husband, imagining him to be jealous of Prince Andrew's memory—or, on the rare occasions, something moved her to sing, a habit she had given up almost entirely since her marriage. In those rare moments when the old fire did kindle in her handsome, fully developed body, she was even more striking than she had been in earlier days.

Since their marriage, Natasha and her husband had lived in Moscow, in Petersburg, on their estate near Moscow, or with her mother—that is, in Nicholas's house. Young Countess Bezukhova was not often seen in society, and those who met her there were not pleased with her, and found her neither charming nor amiable. It was not that Natasha disliked solitude—she did not know herself whether she liked it or not, and actually thought she did not—but between her pregnancies, her confinements, the nursing of her children, and sharing every moment of her husband's life, she had demands on her time that could only be met by giving up society altogether. Everyone who had known Natasha before her marriage marveled at the change in her, as at something extraordinary. Only the old countess, with a mother's instinct, had understood that all Natasha's old outbursts had really sprung from her need for children and a husband—as she herself had once cried out at Otradnoe, half in jest but more than half in earnest—and now the countess was surprised by the surprise of those who had never understood Natasha, and kept saying that she had always known Natasha would make an exemplary wife and mother.
"Only she lets her love of her husband and children overflow every bound," the countess would add, "so much so that it becomes almost absurd."

Natasha did not follow the golden rule advocated by clever people, especially the French, which says a girl should not let herself go once she marries, should not neglect her accomplishments, should be even more careful of her appearance than when she was unmarried, and should set out to charm her husband just as much as she did before he became her husband. Natasha, on the contrary, had at once abandoned all her old powers of attraction, of which her singing had been an unusually potent part. She gave it up precisely because it was so powerfully seductive. She took no trouble over her manners, over refinement of speech, over her toilette, or over showing herself to her husband in her most becoming poses, or over sparing him any inconvenience by not being too demanding. She acted against every one of those rules. She felt that the charms her instinct had once taught her to use would now seem simply ridiculous in her husband's eyes—he to whom, from the very first moment, she had given herself entirely, that is, with her whole soul, leaving no corner of it hidden from him. She felt that what bound her to her husband was not the poetic feelings that had once drawn him to her, but something else—indefinite, yet as firm as the bond between her own body and soul.

To fluff up her curls, put on fashionable dresses, and sing romantic songs in order to charm her husband would have struck her as strange as adorning herself to attract herself. Adorning herself for other people might, perhaps, have been agreeable—she did not know—but she simply had no time at all for it. The chief reason she gave no time to singing, or to dress, or to choosing her words carefully, was that she truly had no time to spare for such things.

We know that a person has the capacity to become completely absorbed in a subject, however trivial it might be, and that there is no subject so trivial that it will not swell to infinite proportions if one's whole attention is fixed on it.

The subject that wholly absorbed Natasha's attention was her family: that is, her husband, whom she had to hold onto so that he would belong entirely to her and to the home, and the children, whom she had to bear, bring into the world, nurse, and raise.

And the more deeply she penetrated into the subject that absorbed her—not with her mind alone, but with her whole soul, her whole being—the larger that subject grew, and the weaker and more inadequate her own powers appeared to her, so that she poured them wholly into that one thing and still could not accomplish everything she believed was needed.

There were, then as now, conversations and arguments about women's rights, about the relations of husband and wife and their freedom and their rights, though these subjects were not yet called "questions" the way they are now; but these topics were not merely uninteresting to Natasha—she simply did not understand them at all.

These questions, then as now, exist only for people who see nothing in marriage but the pleasure married people get from one another—that is, only the beginning of marriage, and not its full meaning, which lies in the family.

Discussions and questions of that kind—rather like the question of how to get the most enjoyment out of one's dinner—did not exist then, and do not exist now, for people whose purpose in eating dinner is the nourishment it provides, just as the purpose of marriage is the family.

If the purpose of dinner is to nourish the body, a man who eats two dinners at once may perhaps enjoy himself more, but he will not achieve his purpose, since his stomach will not be able to digest two dinners.
If the purpose of marriage is the family, then a person who wants many wives or many husbands may perhaps get a great deal of pleasure out of it, but in that case will not have a family.

If the purpose of food is nourishment, and the purpose of marriage is the family, then the whole question comes down to this: not eating more than one can digest, and not having more wives or husbands than are needed for a family—that is, one wife, or one husband. Natasha needed a husband. A husband was given her, and he gave her a family. And not only did she see no need for any other or better husband, but since every power of her soul was bent on serving that husband and that family, she could not imagine, and saw no point in imagining, how things might be if they were different.

Natasha did not care for society in general, but she prized all the more the company of her relatives—Countess Mary, her brother, her mother, and Sonya. She valued the company of those she could come striding to, disheveled, straight from the nursery, still in her dressing gown, to show off, with a joyful face, a yellow stain instead of a green one on the baby's diaper, and from whom she could hear the reassuring words that the baby was much better.

Natasha had let herself go to such an extent that the way she dressed and did her hair, her careless choice of words, and her jealousy—she was jealous of Sonya, of the governess, of every woman, pretty or plain—had become the standing joke of everyone around her. The general opinion was that Pierre was under his wife's thumb, which was in fact perfectly true. From the very first days of their marriage Natasha had made her demands plain. Pierre was greatly surprised by his wife's view—entirely new to him—that every moment of his life belonged to her and to the family. His wife's demands astonished him, but they flattered him too, and he submitted to them.

Pierre's subjection showed itself in the fact that he did not dare so much as flirt with another woman, or even speak to one with a smile; did not dare dine at the club just for amusement; did not dare spend money on a whim; and did not dare stay away for any length of time except on business—under which his wife included his intellectual pursuits, which she did not understand in the least, but to which she attached the greatest importance. To make up for all this, at home Pierre had the right to arrange his own life and that of the whole family exactly as he pleased. At home Natasha placed herself in the position of a slave to her husband, and the whole household walked on tiptoe whenever he was occupied—that is, reading or writing in his study. Pierre had only to show a fondness for something to have it done for him every time, without fail. He had only to express a wish, and Natasha would jump up and run to fulfill it.

The entire household was run according to Pierre's supposed wishes—that is, according to what Natasha guessed his wishes to be. Where and how they lived, their acquaintances and connections, Natasha's own occupations, the children's upbringing—all of it was chosen not merely with an eye to Pierre's stated wishes, but to what Natasha, judging from thoughts he had expressed in conversation, supposed his wishes to be. And she read his real wishes quite correctly, and having once arrived at them, held to them tenaciously. When Pierre himself wanted to change his mind, she would fight him with his own weapons.

So, for instance, in a time of trouble that stayed forever memorable to him, after the birth of their first, delicate child, when they had to change wet nurses three times and Natasha fell ill from despair, Pierre had once told her of Rousseau's view, with which he entirely agreed, that having a wet nurse is unnatural and harmful. When their next baby was born, despite the opposition of her mother, the doctors, and even her own husband—all of whom were strongly against her nursing the baby herself, a thing then unheard of and considered harmful—she insisted on having her own way, and after that nursed every one of her babies herself.

It very often happened that, in a moment's irritation, husband and wife would fall into a dispute, but long afterward Pierre, to his surprise and delight, would find in his wife's ideas and actions the very thought she had argued against, but stripped now of everything superfluous that, in the heat of the dispute, he had piled onto it while stating his own opinion.

After seven years of marriage, Pierre had the joyful, settled certainty that he was not a bad man, and he felt this because he saw himself reflected in his wife. He felt the good and the bad within himself tangled and overlapping. But only what was truly good in him was reflected back in his wife; everything not quite good was cast aside. And this was not the result of any reasoning on her part—it was a direct and mysterious reflection.

title: First Epilogue (1813 - 20) — Chapter 11
paragraphs: Two months before, while Pierre was already staying with the Rostovs, he had received a letter from Prince Theodore, asking him to come to Petersburg to confer on some important questions then being discussed by a society of which Pierre was one of the principal founders.

On reading that letter—she always read her husband's letters—Natasha herself suggested that he go to Petersburg, though his absence would be a real hardship for her. She attached tremendous importance to all her husband's intellectual and abstract concerns, though she did not understand them, and she always dreaded being any hindrance to him in such matters. To Pierre's timid, questioning look after reading the letter she answered by urging him to go, but insisting he fix a definite date for his return. He was given four weeks' leave.
Ever since that leave had run out, more than two weeks before, Natasha had been in a constant state of alarm, low spirits, and irritability.

Denisov, now a retired general and thoroughly dissatisfied with the current state of affairs, had arrived during that fortnight. He looked at Natasha with sorrow and astonishment, as at a poor likeness of someone once dear to him. A dull, dejected look, distracted answers, and talk about the nursery were all he saw and heard from the woman who had once enchanted him.

Natasha was low-spirited and irritable the whole time, most of all when her mother, her brother, Sonya, or Countess Mary, trying to console her, attempted to excuse Pierre and suggest reasons for the delay in his return.

"It's all nonsense, all rubbish—those endless discussions that lead nowhere, and all those idiotic societies!" Natasha would say of the very affairs whose immense importance she herself firmly believed in.

And she would go off to the nursery to nurse Petya, her only boy. Nothing and no one could tell her anything so comforting or so reasonable as this little three-month-old creature, when he lay at her breast and she felt the movement of his lips and the snuffling of his tiny nose. That little creature seemed to say: "You're angry, you're jealous, you'd like to make him pay for it, you're afraid—but here I am! And I am him..." and there was no answering that. It was more than true.

During that anxious fortnight Natasha turned to the baby for comfort so often, and fussed over him so much, that she overfed him, and he fell ill. She was terrified by his illness—and yet that was exactly what she needed. Taken up with worrying over him, she bore her worry about her husband more easily.

She was nursing her boy when the sound of Pierre's sleigh was heard at the front door, and the old nurse—who knew how to please her mistress—came into the room inaudibly, but in a hurry, her face beaming.
"Has he come?" Natasha asked quickly, in a whisper, afraid to move for fear of waking the dozing baby.
"He's come, ma'am," whispered the nurse.

The blood rushed to Natasha's face, and her feet moved of their own accord, but she could not jump up and run out. The baby opened his eyes again and looked at her. "You're here?" he seemed to be saying, and lazily smacked his lips once more.

Carefully drawing her breast away, Natasha rocked him a little, handed him to the nurse, and went toward the door with quick steps. But at the door she stopped, as if her conscience reproached her for abandoning the child so soon in her joy, and she looked back. The nurse, elbows raised, was lifting the baby over the rail of his cot.
"Go on, ma'am! Don't you worry, go!" she whispered, smiling, with the kind of easy familiarity that grows up between a nurse and her mistress.
Natasha ran with quick, light footsteps to the anteroom.
Denisov, who had come out of the study into the dance room with his pipe, now, for the first time, recognized the old Natasha. A flood of bright, joyful light poured from her transfigured face.
"He's come!" she cried as she ran past, and Denisov found that he too was delighted that Pierre, whom he did not much care for, had come home.

Reaching the vestibule, Natasha saw a tall figure in a fur coat unwinding his scarf. "It's him! It's really him! He's come!" she told herself, and, rushing at him, threw her arms around him, pressed his head to her chest, then pushed him back and gazed at his ruddy, happy face, covered in hoarfrost. "Yes, it's him, happy and contented...."

Then all at once she remembered the torment of suspense she had suffered for the last two weeks, and the joy lighting up her face vanished; she frowned and let loose on Pierre a torrent of reproaches and angry words.

"Yes, it's all very well for you. You're pleased, you've had a wonderful time.... But what about me? You might at least have thought of the children. I'm nursing, and my milk went bad.... Petya was at death's door. But you were off enjoying yourself. Yes, enjoying yourself..."

Pierre knew he was not to blame, since he could not have come any sooner; he knew this outburst was unreasonable and would blow over in a minute or two; above all, he knew he himself was cheerful and happy. He wanted to smile, but did not dare even think of it. He made a piteous, frightened face and bowed his head.
"I couldn't help it, on my honor. But how's Petya?"
"He's fine now. Come along! You ought to be ashamed of yourself! If only you could see what I was like without you, how I suffered!"
"You're well?"
"Come, come!" she said, not letting go of his arm. And they went off to their rooms.

When Nicholas and his wife came looking for Pierre, he was in the nursery, holding his baby son, who had woken up again, on his huge right palm, dandling him. A blissful, radiant smile was fixed on the baby's broad face, its mouth open, toothless. The storm had long since passed, and bright, joyful sunshine lit Natasha's face as she gazed tenderly at her husband and child.
"And did you talk everything over well with Prince Theodore?" she asked.
"Yes, splendidly."
"You see, he holds it up." She meant the baby's head. "But how he frightened me... Have you seen the princess? Is it true she's in love with that..."
"Yes, just imagine..."

At that moment Nicholas and Countess Mary came in. Pierre, still holding the baby, bent down, kissed them, and answered their questions. But despite all the interesting things there were to discuss, the baby, in his little cap perched on his unsteady head, plainly held all of Pierre's attention.

"How sweet!" said Countess Mary, looking at and playing with the baby. "Now, Nicholas," she added, turning to her husband, "I simply can't understand how you don't see the charm of these darling little marvels."
"I don't, and I can't," replied Nicholas, looking coldly at the baby. "A lump of flesh. Come along, Pierre!"
"And yet he's such an affectionate father," said Countess Mary, defending her husband, "only once they're a year old or so..."
"Pierre nurses them wonderfully now," said Natasha. "He says his hand was made just for a baby to sit in. Just look!"
"Only not for this..." Pierre suddenly burst out laughing, and, shifting the baby, handed him to the nurse.

title: First Epilogue (1813 - 20) — Chapter 12
paragraphs: As in every large household, at Bald Hills there existed several quite distinct worlds, which merged into one harmonious whole, though each kept its own particular character and made concessions to the others. Every event that took place in that house, joyful or sad, mattered to all these worlds, but each had its own particular reasons for rejoicing or grieving over it, independent of the others.
Pierre's return, for instance, was a joyful and important event, and every one of them felt it to be so.

The servants—the most reliable judges of their masters, since they judge not by what they say or the feelings they express but by their actions and their way of living—were glad of Pierre's return, because they knew that with him around Count Nicholas would stop going out to the estate every single day, and would be in better spirits and a better temper, and also because they would all get handsome presents at the holidays.

The children and their governesses were glad of Pierre's return because no one else drew them into the social life of the household the way he did. He alone could play, on the clavichord, that écossaise—his only piece—to which, as he said, every possible kind of dance could be danced, and they felt certain he had brought presents for every one of them.

Young Nicholas, now a slim, delicate boy of fifteen with intelligent eyes and curly light-brown hair, was thrilled, because Uncle Pierre, as he called him, was the object of his rapturous, passionate devotion. No one had planted this love of Pierre in him; he saw him only now and then. Countess Mary, who had raised him, had done everything she could to make him love her husband the way she loved him, and little Nicholas did love his uncle, but with just a shade of contempt mixed in. Pierre, though, he adored. He did not want to be a hussar or a Knight of St. George like Uncle Nicholas; he wanted to be learned, and wise, and kind, like Pierre. In Pierre's presence his face always lit up with pleasure, and he would flush and go breathless whenever Pierre spoke to him. He never missed a single word Pierre said, and would afterward, with Dessalles or alone, recall and turn over in his mind the meaning of everything Pierre had said. Pierre's past life, and his unhappiness before 1812—of which young Nicholas had formed a vague, poetic picture from a few words he had overheard—his adventures in Moscow, his captivity, Platon Karataev, of whom he had heard from Pierre, his love for Natasha, of whom the boy was also especially fond, and above all Pierre's friendship with the father Nicholas could not remember—all of it made Pierre, in his eyes, a hero and a saint.

From scraps overheard about Natasha and his father, from the emotion with which Pierre spoke of that dead father, and from the careful, reverent tenderness with which Natasha spoke of him, the boy, only just beginning to guess what love was, had formed the idea that his father had loved Natasha, and, dying, had left her to his friend. But the father the boy could not remember appeared to him as a kind of divinity he could not picture, one he never thought of without his heart swelling and tears of sadness and rapture coming to his eyes. And so the boy, too, was happy that Pierre had arrived.
The guests welcomed Pierre because he always helped enliven and bring together whatever company he found himself in.
The grown members of the family, not to mention his wife, were glad to have back a friend whose presence made life run more smoothly and peacefully.
The old ladies were pleased with the presents he brought them, and, above all, that Natasha would now go back to being herself.
Pierre sensed the different expectations of all these different worlds, and hurried to satisfy them all.

Absent-minded and forgetful as he was, the most absent-minded and forgetful of men, Pierre, with the help of a list his wife had drawn up, had now bought everything—not forgetting his mother- and brother-in-law's commissions, nor the dress material meant as a present for Belova, nor the toys for his wife's nephews. In the early days of their marriage it had struck him as strange that his wife should expect him not to forget to buy every single thing he had undertaken to buy, and he had been taken aback by her real annoyance the first time he came home from a trip having forgotten everything. But in time he grew used to this expectation. Knowing that Natasha never asked anything for herself, and only gave him commissions for others when he himself had first offered to take them on, he now found an unexpected, almost childlike pleasure in buying presents for everyone in the house, and never forgot a single one. If Natasha found fault with him now, it was only for buying too much, and things that were too expensive. To her other supposed faults—untidiness and neglect of her own appearance, faults most people saw as such but which Pierre thought of as qualities—she had now added stinginess.

From the time Pierre began living as a family man, on a footing that meant heavy expenses, he had noticed, to his surprise, that he spent only half what he used to, and that his affairs—which had been in disorder lately, chiefly because of his first wife's debts—had begun to improve.

Life had become cheaper because it was more confined: that most expensive luxury of all, the kind of life that can be changed at any moment, was no longer his, and he no longer wanted it. He felt that his way of life had now been settled once and for all, until death, and that it was no longer in his power to change it, and so, in that sense, his way of life had turned out to be economical.
With a merry, smiling face, Pierre was sorting through his purchases.
"What do you think of this?" he said, unrolling a piece of cloth like a shopkeeper.
Natasha, sitting across from him with her eldest daughter on her lap, turned her sparkling eyes swiftly from her husband to the things he was showing her.
"That's for Belova? Excellent!" She felt the quality of the material. "A ruble an arshin, I suppose?"
Pierre told her the price.

"Too dear!" Natasha said. "How pleased the children will be, and Mamma too! Only you needn't have bought me this," she added, unable to hold back a smile as she gazed admiringly at a gold comb set with pearls, of a kind just then coming into fashion.
"Adele tempted me: she kept insisting I buy it," Pierre answered.
"When am I supposed to wear it?" and Natasha stuck it into her coil of hair. "When I take little Masha into society? Maybe it'll be fashionable again by then. Well, come along now."
And, gathering up the presents, they went first to the nursery, and then to the old countess's rooms.
The countess was sitting with her companion Belova, playing a game of grand-patience as usual, when Pierre and Natasha came into the drawing room with parcels under their arms.
The countess was now past sixty, entirely gray, and wore a cap with a frill framing her face. Her face had shriveled, her upper lip had sunk in, and her eyes had grown dim.

After the deaths of her son and her husband in such quick succession, she felt herself a person accidentally forgotten by the world, left with no aim or purpose for her existence. She ate, drank, slept, or lay awake, but she did not live. Life gave her no new impressions. She wanted nothing from life but peace, and only death could give her that peace. But until death came she had to go on living—that is, to keep using her vital forces. A peculiarity one notices in very small children and very old people alike was especially plain in her. Her life had no outward aims left—only a need to keep exercising her various functions and inclinations remained visible. She had to eat, sleep, think, speak, weep, work, vent her anger, and so on, simply because she had a stomach, a brain, muscles, nerves, and a liver. She did none of these things under any outward pressure, the way people in the full vigor of life do, for whom the purpose behind exercising their own functions goes unnoticed, hidden behind whatever goal they're chasing. She talked only because she had a physical need to exercise her tongue and lungs. She cried the way a child cries, because her nose needed clearing, and so on. What is a goal, for people in full vigor, was for her plainly nothing but a pretext.
So, in the mornings—especially if she had eaten something rich the day before—she would feel a need to be angry, and would seize on the handiest pretext: Belova's deafness.
She would begin saying something to her, in a low voice, from the far end of the room.
"It seems a little warmer today, my dear," she would murmur.
And when Belova answered, "Oh yes, they've come," she would mutter angrily: "Good Lord! How stupid and deaf she is!"

Another pretext would be her snuff, which would seem too dry, or too damp, or not ground fine enough. After these fits of irritation her face would turn yellow, and her maids knew, by unfailing signs, exactly when Belova would be deaf again, the snuff damp again, and the countess's face yellow again. Just as she needed to work off her ill temper, so too she sometimes needed to exercise her still-surviving faculty of thought—and the pretext for that was a game of patience. When she needed to cry, the late count would serve as pretext. When she wanted to be agitated, Nicholas and his health would be the pretext, and when she felt the need to speak spitefully, Countess Mary would serve. When her vocal organs needed exercise, usually around seven o'clock, once she had rested after dinner in a darkened room, the pretext would be retelling the same old stories over and over to the same listeners.

The old lady's condition was understood by the whole household, though no one ever spoke of it aloud, and everyone made every possible effort to see to her needs. Only in a rare glance, exchanged with a sad smile between Nicholas, Pierre, Natasha, and Countess Mary, was their shared understanding of her condition ever expressed.

But those glances said something more besides: they said that she had already played her part in life, that what they now saw before them was not the whole of her, that all of them must one day become like her, and that they were glad to give way to her, to hold themselves back for the sake of this once-precious person, once as full of life as they themselves now were, but now so much to be pitied. "Memento mori," said those glances.
Only the truly heartless, the stupid ones in that household, and the very young children failed to understand this, and steered clear of her.

title: First Epilogue (1813 - 20) — Chapter 13
paragraphs: When Pierre and his wife came into the drawing room, the countess was in one of her usual moods, the kind that needed the mental effort of a game of patience, and so—though out of sheer habit she greeted him with the words she always used whenever Pierre or her son came back after an absence: "High time, my dear, high time! We were all tired of waiting for you. Well, thank God!" and received her presents with another of her customary remarks: "It's not the gift that matters, my dear, but that you gave it to me, an old woman..."—still, it was plain she was not really pleased at Pierre's arrival just then, since it drew her attention away from the unfinished game.

She finished her game of patience before she even examined the presents. They consisted of a card box of splendid workmanship, a bright-blue Sèvres teacup painted with shepherdesses and fitted with a lid, and a gold snuffbox with the count's portrait on the lid, which Pierre had commissioned from a miniaturist in Petersburg. The countess had long wanted a box of just that kind, but, not wanting to cry just then, she glanced indifferently at the portrait and gave her chief attention to the card box.

"Thank you, my dear, you've cheered me up," she said, as she always did. "But best of all, you've brought yourself back—I never saw anything like it, you really ought to give your wife a scolding!
