What are we to do with her? She's like a madwoman when you're away. Doesn't see anything, doesn't remember anything," she went on, repeating her usual phrases. "Look, Anna Timofeyevna," she added, turning to her companion, "see what a card box my son has brought us!"
Belova admired the presents and was delighted with her dress material.

Though Pierre, Natasha, Nicholas, Countess Mary, and Denisov had a great deal to talk over that they could not discuss in front of the old countess—not that anything was hidden from her, but because she had fallen so far behind in so many things that if they had started talking in her presence, they would have had to answer questions that made no sense anymore, and repeat things they had already told her many times over: that so-and-so was dead, that so-and-so had married, all of which she would once again be unable to remember—still, out of habit, they all sat down to tea around the samovar in the drawing room, and Pierre answered the countess's questions about whether Prince Vasili had aged, and whether Countess Mary Alexeyevna sent her greetings and still thought of them, and other matters that interested no one, including the countess herself.

This kind of conversation, interesting to no one and yet unavoidable, went on all through teatime. All the grown members of the family had gathered around the round tea table, where Sonya presided over the samovar. The children, with their tutors and governesses, had already had their tea, and their voices could be heard from the next room. At tea, everyone sat in their accustomed places: Nicholas by the stove, at a small table where his tea was brought to him; Milka, the old gray borzoi bitch, daughter of the first Milka, her face now quite gray and her large black eyes seeming more prominent than ever, lay in the armchair beside him; Denisov, his curly hair, mustache, and whiskers now half gray, sat beside Countess Mary, his general's tunic unbuttoned; Pierre sat between his wife and the old countess. He talked about the things he knew would interest the old lady and that she could follow. He told her of goings-on in society, and about the people who had once made up the circle of her contemporaries, a real, living, distinct group, but who were now for the most part scattered about the world, and, like herself, were gathering in the last ears of the harvests they had sown in earlier years. But to the old countess, those contemporaries of hers still seemed the only serious, real society there was. Natasha could tell, from how animated Pierre was, that his visit had been eventful and that he had a great deal to tell them, but did not dare say it in front of the old countess. Denisov, not being a member of the family, did not grasp Pierre's caution, and, being a malcontent deeply interested in what was going on in Petersburg, kept pressing Pierre to tell them what was happening in the Semyonovsky regiment, then about Arakcheev, then about the Bible Society. Once or twice Pierre got carried away and began speaking of these things, but Nicholas and Natasha always steered him back to the health of Prince Ivan and Countess Mary Alexeyevna.
"Well, and all this idiocy—Gossner and Tatáwinova? Is that weally still going on?" Denisov asked.
"Going on?" Pierre exclaimed. "Why, more than ever! The Bible Society is running the whole government now!"

"What's that, mon cher ami?" asked the countess, who had finished her tea and plainly needed a pretext for being angry now that her meal was done. "What's this about the government? I don't understand."

"Well, you know, Maman," Nicholas put in, knowing just how to translate things into his mother's language, "Prince Alexander Golitsyn has founded a society, and as a result he has great influence, they say."
"Arakcheev and Golitsyn," Pierre put in, without thinking, "are the whole government now! And what a government! They see treason everywhere and are afraid of everything."

"Well, and how is Prince Alexander to blame? He's a most estimable man. I used to meet him at Mary Antonovna's," the countess said, in an offended tone; and, still more offended that everyone had fallen silent, she went on: "These days everyone finds fault with everything. A Gospel Society! Well, and what's the harm in that?" and she rose—everyone else got up too—and, with a stern expression, sailed back to her table in the sitting room.
The melancholy silence that followed was broken by the sound of the children's voices and laughter from the next room. Some jolly commotion was plainly going on there.
"Finished, finished!" little Natasha's gleeful shriek rose above the rest.
Pierre exchanged glances with Countess Mary and Nicholas—he never once lost sight of Natasha—and smiled happily.
"That's delightful music!" he said.
"It means Anna Makarovna has finished her stocking," said Countess Mary.

"Oh, I'll go and see," said Pierre, jumping up. "You know," he added, stopping at the door, "why I'm especially fond of that music? It's always the first thing that tells me all is well. When I was driving here today, the closer I got to the house, the more anxious I grew. As soon as I stepped into the anteroom, I heard Andrusha's peals of laughter, and I knew right then that everything was fine."
"I know! I know that feeling," said Nicholas. "But I mustn't go in there—those stockings are supposed to be a surprise for me."
Pierre went off to the children, and the shouting and laughter grew louder still.

"Come, Anna Makarovna," Pierre's voice could be heard saying, "come here, into the middle of the room, and at the word of command, 'One, two'—and when I say 'three'... You stand here, and you in my arms—now then! One, two!..." said Pierre, and a silence fell: "three!"—and a rapturous, breathless shout of children's voices filled the room. "Two, two!" they shouted.

This meant two stockings, which, by some secret method known only to herself, Anna Makarovna would knit at the same time on the same needles, and which, once they were finished, she would always draw out triumphantly, one from inside the other, right in front of the children.

title: First Epilogue (1813 - 20) — Chapter 14
paragraphs: Soon after this the children came in to say good night. They kissed everyone, the tutors and governesses made their bows, and they went out. Only young Nicholas and his tutor stayed behind. Dessalles whispered to the boy to come downstairs.
"No, Monsieur Dessalles, I'll ask my aunt to let me stay," answered Nicholas Bolkonsky, also in a whisper.
"Ma tante, please let me stay," he said, going up to his aunt.
His face was full of entreaty, agitation, and ecstasy. Countess Mary glanced at him and turned to Pierre.
"When you're here, he can't tear himself away," she said.

"I'll bring him to you directly, Monsieur Dessalles. Good night!" said Pierre, offering his hand to the Swiss tutor, and then he turned to young Nicholas with a smile. "You and I haven't had a proper look at each other yet.... How he's grown to look like him, Mary!" he added, turning to Countess Mary.
"Like my father?" the boy asked, flushing crimson, looking up at Pierre with bright, rapturous eyes.

Pierre nodded, and went on with what he had been saying before the children interrupted. Countess Mary sat down to her woolwork; Natasha never took her eyes off her husband. Nicholas and Denisov got up, asked for their pipes, smoked, went to fetch more tea from Sonya, who sat weary but resolute at the samovar, and put questions to Pierre. The curly-headed, delicate boy sat unnoticed in a corner, his eyes shining, starting every now and then and muttering something under his breath, clearly caught up in some new and powerful feeling as he kept turning his curly head, with its thin neck bared by his turned-down collar, toward the place where Pierre sat.

The conversation turned to the current gossip about those in power—the subject most people find of greatest interest in domestic politics. Denisov, dissatisfied with the government on account of his own disappointments in the service, listened with pleasure to the things being done in Petersburg, things that struck him as foolish, and made sharp, forceful remarks on everything Pierre told them.

"One used to have to be German—now one has to dance attendance on Tatáwinova and Madame Kwüdener, and wead Ecka'tshausen and the bwethwen. Oh, they should just turn that fine fellow Bonaparte loose again—he'd knock all this nonsense out of them! Fancy giving command of the Semyonov wegiment to a fellow like that Schwa'tz!" he cried.

Nicholas, though he lacked Denisov's readiness to find fault with everything, also thought that discussing the government was a very serious, weighty matter, and it seemed to him a matter of real importance that A had been appointed Minister of This, and B Governor General of That, and that the Emperor had said such and such, and this minister had said such and such. And so he thought it his duty to take an interest in these things, and questioned Pierre closely. The questions the two of them put kept the conversation from straying beyond its ordinary character—gossip about the upper reaches of government.

But Natasha, who knew all her husband's ways and ideas, could see that he had long been wanting, without managing it, to steer the conversation onto another track and give voice to the idea he felt so deeply, the very idea for whose sake he had gone to Petersburg to consult with his new friend Prince Theodore, and she came to his aid by asking how things had gone with Prince Theodore.
"What was it about?" asked Nicholas.

"Always the same thing," said Pierre, glancing around at his listeners. "Everyone can see things have gotten so bad that they can't go on this way any longer, and that it's the duty of every decent man to work against it as far as he can."
"What can decent men do?" Nicholas asked, frowning slightly. "What is there to be done?"
"Well, this..."
"Come into my study," said Nicholas.

Natasha, who had long expected to be sent for to nurse her baby, now heard the nurse calling her and went off to the nursery. Countess Mary followed her. The men went into the study, and little Nicholas Bolkonsky, unnoticed by his uncle, followed them in and sat down at the writing table, in a shadowy corner by the window.
"Well, what would you do?" asked Denisov.
"Always some fantastic scheme or other," said Nicholas.

"Why this," Pierre began, not sitting down but pacing the room, sometimes stopping short, gesturing, and lisping: "the situation in Petersburg is this. The Emperor pays no attention to anything anymore. He's given himself over entirely to this mysticism"—Pierre could no longer stand mysticism in anyone—"he only wants peace, and only these people, sans foi ni loi,* can give it to him—people who go around recklessly hacking and strangling everything: Magnitsky, Arakcheev, and the rest of that crowd.... You'll agree that if you didn't oversee your own estates yourself, and only wanted a quiet life, the harsher your steward was, the more easily your object would be achieved," he said to Nicholas.
* Without faith or law.
"Well, and where does that lead?" said Nicholas.

"Well, everything is going to ruin! Robbery in the law courts, nothing in the army but flogging, drilling, and Military Settlements; the people are being tormented, education is being crushed. Everything young and honest is being ground down! Everyone can see this can't go on. Everything is stretched so tight that it's bound to snap," said Pierre—much as everyone who has ever examined the actions of any government has said, since governments began. "I told them just one thing, in Petersburg."
"Told whom?"

"Well, you know whom," said Pierre, with a meaningful glance from under his brows. "Prince Theodore and the rest of them. Encouraging culture and philanthropy is all very well, of course. The aim is excellent—but under the present circumstances, something else is needed."
At that moment Nicholas noticed his nephew was in the room. His face darkened, and he went up to the boy.
"Why are you in here?"

"Why? Let him stay," said Pierre, taking Nicholas by the arm and going on. "That's not enough, I told them. Something else is needed. When you're standing there expecting the overstretched string to snap at any moment, when everyone is expecting the inevitable catastrophe, then as many people as possible need to join hands, as tightly as they can, to stand against the coming disaster. Everything young and strong is being lured away and corrupted. One man is drawn off by women, another by honors, a third by ambition or money, and off they go, over to that camp. There are no independent men left—men like you or me. What I'm saying is: widen the scope of our society, let the watchword be not virtue alone, but independence and action as well!"
Nicholas, who had let go of his nephew, irritably pulled up an armchair, sat down in it, and listened to Pierre, coughing with displeasure and frowning more and more.
"But action toward what end?" he burst out. "And what position would you take toward the government?"

"Why, the position of helpers. The society needn't be secret at all, if the government allows it. It's not just not hostile to the government—it's a society of true conservatives, a society of gentlemen in the fullest sense of the word. Its whole purpose is to stop some Pugachev or other from murdering my children and yours, and to stop Arakcheev from sending me off to some Military Settlement. We join hands only for the public good and the general safety."
"Yes, but it's a secret society, and so a hostile one, a harmful one, one that can only do harm."

"Why? Did the Tugendbund, which saved Europe"—they did not yet dare suggest that it was Russia that had saved Europe—"do any harm? The Tugendbund is an alliance of virtue: it's love, mutual aid... it's what Christ preached on the Cross."

Natasha, who had come in during the conversation, looked happily at her husband. It was not what he was saying that pleased her—that did not even interest her, since to her it all seemed extremely simple, and she felt she had known it for a long time, because she knew it sprang from Pierre's whole soul—but it was his animated, enthusiastic look that made her glad.

The boy with the thin neck rising from his turned-down collar—whom everyone had forgotten about—watched Pierre with even greater and more rapturous delight. Every word Pierre spoke burned itself into his heart, and, with a nervous movement of his fingers, he found himself unconsciously breaking the sealing wax and the quill pens that came to hand on his uncle's table.
"It isn't at all what you think; but that's what the German Tugendbund was, and it's what I'm proposing."

"No, my fwiend! The Tugendbund's all vewy well for sausage eaters, but I don't understand it and can't even pwonounce it," Denisov broke in, loudly and firmly. "I agwee that evewything here is wotten and howwible, but the Tugendbund I don't understand. If we're not satisfied, let's have a wevolt of our own. That's fine by me. Je suis vot'e homme!"*
* "I'm your man."

Pierre smiled, Natasha burst out laughing, but Nicholas only knitted his brows further, and set about proving to Pierre that there was no real prospect of any great change, and that all the danger Pierre spoke of existed only in his own imagination. Pierre argued the opposite, and, since his mental powers were greater and more resourceful, Nicholas found himself cornered. This only made him angrier still, since he was fully convinced—not by reasoning, but by something inside him stronger than reason—of the rightness of his own view.

"I'll tell you this," he said, standing up and trying, with nervously twitching fingers, to prop his pipe up in a corner, then finally giving up the attempt. "I can't prove it to you. You say everything here is rotten, and that a collapse is coming: I don't see it. But you also say our oath of allegiance is some kind of conditional thing, and to that I say: 'You are my best friend, as you well know, but if you formed a secret society and started working against the government—whatever government it may be—I know it's my duty to obey the government. And if Arakcheev ordered me to lead a squadron against you and cut you down, I wouldn't hesitate an instant, and I'd do it.' Argue about that all you like!"

An awkward silence followed these words. Natasha was the first to speak, defending her husband and attacking her brother. Her defense was weak and clumsy, but it did what she wanted. The conversation started up again, no longer in the unpleasantly hostile tone of Nicholas's last words.
When they all got up to go in to supper, little Nicholas Bolkonsky went up to Pierre, pale, his eyes shining and radiant.
"Uncle Pierre, you... no... If Papa were alive... would he agree with you?" he asked.

And Pierre suddenly grasped what a special, independent, complicated, and powerful process of thought and feeling must have been going on in this boy throughout the whole conversation, and, remembering everything he had said, he wished the lad had not heard him. Still, he had to give him some answer.
"Yes, I think so," he said, reluctantly, and left the study.
The boy looked down and seemed only now to notice what he had done to the things on the table. He flushed and went up to Nicholas.
"Uncle, forgive me, I did that... without meaning to," he said, pointing to the broken sealing wax and pens.
Nicholas started angrily.
"All right, all right," he said, throwing the bits under the table.
And, plainly holding back his irritation with some effort, he turned away from the boy.
"You shouldn't have been in here at all," he said.

title: First Epilogue (1813 - 20) — Chapter 15
paragraphs: The talk at supper was not about politics or secret societies, but turned to the subject Nicholas liked best of all—memories of 1812. Denisov set it going, and Pierre was particularly agreeable and amusing on the subject. The family parted for the night on the friendliest terms.

After supper Nicholas, having undressed in his study and given his instructions to the steward, who had been waiting for him, went to the bedroom in his dressing gown, where he found his wife still at her table, writing.
"What are you writing, Mary?" Nicholas asked.
Countess Mary blushed. She was afraid that what she was writing would not be understood or approved of by her husband.
She had wanted to keep what she was writing hidden from him, but at the same time she was glad he had caught her at it, glad that she would now have to tell him.
"A diary, Nicholas," she answered, handing him a blue exercise book filled with her firm, bold handwriting.
"A diary?" Nicholas repeated, with a touch of irony, and picked up the book.
It was written in French.

December 4. Today when Andrusha (her eldest boy) woke up, he did not want to dress, and Mademoiselle Louise sent for me. He was naughty and stubborn. I tried threats, but that only made him angrier. So I took the matter in hand: I left him alone and, with nurse's help, began getting the other children up, telling him I did not love him. For a long time he was silent, as if astonished, then he jumped out of bed, ran to me in his shirt, and sobbed so hard that I could not calm him for a long time. It was plain that what troubled him most was that he had grieved me. Later, in the evening, when I gave him his ticket, he again began to cry piteously and kiss me. One can get him to do anything through tenderness.
"What's a 'ticket'?" Nicholas asked.
"I've started giving the older ones marks every evening, showing how they've behaved."

Nicholas looked into the radiant eyes gazing up at him, and went on turning the pages and reading. In the diary, everything in the children's lives that had struck their mother as worth noting, whether as a sign of their character or as the basis for some general reflection on methods of upbringing, had been set down. Most of it was insignificant trifles, but they did not seem so either to the mother or, now, reading this diary about his own children for the first time, to the father.
Under the date "5" was entered:

Mitya was naughty at table. Papa said he was to have no pudding. He had none, but he looked so unhappily and greedily at the others while they were eating! I think that punishing children by depriving them of sweets only makes them greedier. Must tell Nicholas this.

Nicholas set the book down and looked at his wife. The radiant eyes gazed back at him questioningly: would he approve of her diary, or disapprove? There could be no doubt of his approval—or of his admiration for his wife.

Perhaps it needn't be done quite so pedantically, Nicholas thought, or even be done at all, but this tireless, unceasing spiritual effort, whose only aim was the children's moral welfare, delighted him. Had Nicholas been able to put his feelings into words, he would have found that his steady, tender, proud love for his wife rested on his sense of wonder at her spiritual depth, and at the lofty moral world, almost beyond his own reach, in which she had her being.

He was proud of her intelligence and her goodness, recognized his own insignificance beside her in that spiritual world, and rejoiced all the more that a soul like hers not only belonged to him, but was part of himself.

"I quite, quite approve, my dearest!" he said, with a meaningful look, and, after a short pause, added: "And I behaved badly today. You weren't in the study. We got into an argument—Pierre and I—and I lost my temper. But he's impossible: such a child! I don't know what would become of him if Natasha didn't keep him in hand.... Do you have any idea why he went to Petersburg? They've formed..."
"Yes, I know," said Countess Mary. "Natasha told me."

"Well then, you know," Nicholas went on, growing hot all over again just remembering their discussion, "he wanted to convince me it's every honest man's duty to go against the government, and that the oath of allegiance and one's duty... I'm sorry you weren't there. They all fell on me—Denisov and Natasha... Natasha is absurd. The way she rules over him! And yet the moment there's an actual argument, she has no words of her own, only repeats his," added Nicholas, giving in to that irresistible urge that tempts us to sit in judgment over the people closest and dearest to us. He forgot that what he was saying about Natasha could be applied, word for word, to himself, in relation to his own wife.
"Yes, I've noticed that," said Countess Mary.
"When I told him that duty and the oath stand above everything, he set about proving I don't know what! A pity you weren't there—what would you have said?"

"As I see it, you were quite right, and I told Natasha so. Pierre says everyone is suffering, being tormented and corrupted, and that it's our duty to help our neighbor. Of course he's right about that," said Countess Mary, "but he forgets that we have other duties closer to home, duties God Himself has laid on us, and that though we might risk ourselves, we mustn't risk our children."

"Yes, that's it exactly! That's just what I told him," put in Nicholas, who fancied he really had said it. "But they kept insisting on their own view—love of one's neighbor and Christianity—and all this in front of young Nicholas, who had come into my study and broken every single thing there."

"Ah, Nicholas, do you know, I'm often troubled about little Nicholas," said Countess Mary. "He's such an unusual boy. I'm afraid I neglect him for the sake of my own children: we all have children, relations, while he has no one at all. He's always alone with his own thoughts."

"Well, I don't think you have anything to reproach yourself for on his account. Everything the fondest mother could do for her son, you have done and are doing for him, and of course I'm glad of it. He's a fine boy, a fine boy! This evening he listened to Pierre as if in a trance, and just imagine—as we were going in to supper, I looked, and he'd broken everything on my table to bits, and he told me about it himself, right away! I've never known him to tell a lie. A fine boy, a fine boy!" Nicholas repeated, though at heart he was not particularly fond of Nicholas Bolkonsky, but was always eager to acknowledge that he was a fine boy.

"Still, I'm not the same as his own mother would be," said Countess Mary. "I feel that I'm not, and it troubles me. A wonderful boy, but I'm dreadfully afraid for him. It would do him good to have some companions."

"Well, it won't be for long. Next summer I'll take him to Petersburg," said Nicholas. "Yes, Pierre always was a dreamer, and always will be," he went on, returning to the talk in the study, which had plainly unsettled him. "Well, what business is it of mine what goes on there—whether Arakcheev is bad, or any of that? What business was it of mine when I got married and was so deep in debt I was threatened with prison, and had a mother who couldn't see or understand any of it? And then there's you, and the children, and our own affairs. Do you think it's for my own pleasure that I'm out at the farm, or in the office, from morning till night? No, but I know I have to work, to comfort my mother, to repay you, and not to leave the children beggars the way I was."

Countess Mary wanted to tell him that man does not live by bread alone, and that he attached too much importance to these matters. But she knew she must not say this, and that it would be no use saying it. She only took his hand and kissed it. He took this as a sign of approval, a confirmation of his own thinking, and after a few minutes' reflection went on thinking aloud.
"You know, Mary, today Elias Mitrofanych"—this was his steward—"came back from the Tambov estate and told me they're already offering eighty thousand rubles for the forest."
And, his face eager, Nicholas began talking about the possibility of buying back Otradnoe before long, and added: "Another ten years of life, and I'll leave the children... in an excellent position."

Countess Mary listened to her husband and took in everything he told her. She knew that when he thought aloud like this, he would sometimes ask her what he had just been saying, and be annoyed if he noticed she had been thinking about something else. But she had to force herself to pay attention, because what he was saying did not interest her in the least. She looked at him, and instead of thinking, she felt something different. She felt a submissive, tender love for this man, who would never understand everything she understood, and this seemed to make her love for him even stronger, adding to it a touch of passionate tenderness. Besides this feeling, which absorbed her wholly and kept her from following the details of her husband's plans, thoughts unconnected with anything he was saying drifted through her mind. She thought of her nephew. Her husband's account of how agitated the boy had been while Pierre was speaking struck her forcibly, and various traits of his gentle, sensitive character came back to her; and thinking of her nephew, she found herself thinking of her own children too. She did not compare them with him, but compared her feeling for them with her feeling for him, and felt, with some regret, that something was lacking in her feeling for young Nicholas.

Sometimes it seemed to her that this difference came simply from the difference in their ages, but she felt herself at fault toward him, and promised herself, in her heart, to do better, to achieve the impossible—to love, in this life, her husband, her children, little Nicholas, and all her neighbors, as Christ loved mankind. Countess Mary's soul always strove toward the infinite, the eternal, the absolute, and so could never be at peace. A stern expression, marking the lofty, secret suffering of a soul weighed down by the body, showed on her face. Nicholas looked at her. "O God! What will become of us if she dies, as I always fear when her face looks like that?" he thought, and, placing himself before the icon, he began to say his evening prayers.
